system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Exponential information gathering
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: The EIG algorithm for synchronous Byzantine agreement in f+1 rounds with n ≥ 3f+1. Covers the tree of reported values, recursive majority reconstruction, the common-node correctness argument, and the n > 3f lower bound it matches. Excludes phase king, except as a contrast on message size.

ATOMS:
- CS-DIST-C08-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: EIG gives a Byzantine agreement algorithm that runs in $f+1$ synchronous rounds and guarantees agreement and validity as long as $n \ge 3f+1$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0113-s03] 10.2.1 Exponential information gathering gets n = 3f + 1
    [CS-DIST-p0113-s08] This technique was used by Pease, Shostak, and Lamport [PSL80] to show that their impossibility result is tight: there exists an algorithm for Byzantine agreement that runs in f + 1 synchronous rounds and guarantees agreement and validity as long as n ≥3f + 1.
- CS-DIST-C08-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Exponential information gathering (EIG) is a synchronous Byzantine agreement technique in which each process gossips, and its state is a tree recording who heard what from. The tree is built from pairs ⟨path, input⟩, where path is a sequence of intermediaries with no repetitions.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0113-s04] The idea of exponential information gathering is that each process will do a lot of gossiping, but now its state is no longer just a ﬂat set of inputs, but a tree describing who it heard what from.
    [CS-DIST-p0113-s05] We build this tree out of pairs of the form ⟨path, input⟩where path is a sequence of intermediaries with no repetitions and input is some input.
- CS-DIST-C08-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: Exponential information gathering gives a synchronous Byzantine agreement algorithm that runs in $f+1$ rounds and guarantees agreement and validity as long as $n \ge 3f+1$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0113-s08] This technique was used by Pease, Shostak, and Lamport [PSL80] to show that their impossibility result is tight: there exists an algorithm for Byzantine agreement that runs in f + 1 synchronous rounds and guarantees agreement and validity as long as n ≥3f + 1.
- CS-DIST-C08-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: EIG achieves agreement through the notion of a common node, one where all non-faulty processes compute the same $val^*$. Every root-to-leaf path has a common node because it passes through $f+1$ labels and at least one is good. A node whose children are all common is itself common, so a non-common root would force a path with no common node, which is impossible.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0116-s10] Agreement: Observe that every path has a common node on it, since a path travels through f +1 nodes and one of them is good.
    [CS-DIST-p0116-s11] If we then suppose that the root is not common: by Lemma 10.2.3, it must have a not-common child, that node must have a not-common child, etc.
    [CS-DIST-p0116-s12] But this constructs a path from the root to a leaf with no not-common nodes, which we just proved can’t happen.
- CS-DIST-C08-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: No algorithm can solve Byzantine agreement with $n=3f$ processes. The $n=3$, $f=1$ case is impossible, and a protocol for $n=3f$ would yield one for $n=3$, $f=1$ by letting each of 3 processes simulate a group of $f$ processes that all share the same input.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0110-s10] Suppose that there were an algorithm that solved Byzantine agreement with n = 3f processes.
    [CS-DIST-p0110-s11] Group the processes into groups of size f, and let each of the n = 3 processes simulate one group, with everybody in the group getting the same input, which can only make things easier.
    [CS-DIST-p0110-s12] Then we get a protocol for n = 3 and f = 1, an impossibility.
- CS-DIST-C08-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: When exponential information gathering is applied in the Byzantine model, ill-formed or missing messages from a process are replaced by default values, but otherwise the data-collecting part proceeds as in the crash failure model.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0113-s14] To apply EIG in the Byzantine model, ill-formed or missing messages from j are replaced by default values, but otherwise the data-collecting part of EIG proceeds as in the crash failure model.
